corrections.proposed: relocated to the Marine Museum of Manitoba, Selkirk, 1989
corrections.why: Selkirk Museum, Rowlett and ARLHS all say the original tower moved to Selkirk; the island now has a mast light. The Wikidata-based record still says the tower stands on the island.

corrections.proposed: active as a mast light on the island; the original tower is a museum exhibit
corrections.why: The record's status reads as if the historic tower still works on the island. The 2020 mast light is the active aid; the historic tower is preserved.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Marine Museum history says Matheson built the 1898 tower; Lighthouse Friends and Selkirk name John W. Scott as contractor and Matheson as the keeper hired in 1899. The story follows the contractor account.
The record's conflicting statuses (active, inactive) are explained by the move to Selkirk in 1989 and the mast light shown on the island in 2020.

notes_for_editor: 1) The 1898 announcement, the Scott contract and the first lighting come from Lighthouse Friends quoting the Department's 1898 report. The local corpus of Canadian marine reports starts in 1900, so this report was not checked. 2) The keeper date (D. Matheson, June 22, 1899) was checked on the page image of the 1915 report (scan p.77): the Black Bear island row carries it. The 1911-12 table (scan p.256) lists 'Black Bear Island Win. Hughes Feb. 12, 1892' in the same run; Hughes was the Red River keeper by Selkirk's account, so that line is probably misaligned and is not used. 3) The Marine Museum (MHS) credits Matheson with building the tower and calls the island 'Black Island'; this conflicts with Lighthouse Friends and Selkirk and is noted in the story. 4) The 1989 move date comes from Selkirk's source list (Selkirk Journal, 23 May 1989, p. 15), which was not read; the story says Selkirk's history lists it among its sources. 5) The University of Manitoba PDF on Black Bear Island was not read: it is blocked by a bot check. 6) Wikidata's record (tower standing on the island, 8 m, status active) conflicts with ARLHS, Rowlett and Selkirk; the corrections propose the change for a human to check. Lighthouse Friends describes the mast light as flashing white; Rowlett's entry gives a quick-flashing white light with a focal plane of 13 m, which the story does not repeat. 7) Lighthouse Friends' notes on the foghorn and the 1919 salary are attributed; the 1919 quote is copied with its odd wording ('the least year of his service'). 8) Keepers after 1937 are not known from these sources. 9) Fact-check 2026-10-28: the story no longer says the mast showed a light 'instead' of the tower; the 1914 light is described as one of the pair on the museum grounds, per the museum's history; the 'World List' name is corrected to ARLHS; the Coast Guard-style claims are footnoted.
